lesson.title: Golden Rain: Watching Precipitation Reactions Happen
lesson.summary: A precipitation reaction is a double replacement reaction in which mixing two clear solutions produces an insoluble solid, called a precipitate, that separates out and can be seen, filtered, or weighed.
lesson.body:
Double Replacement taught you that mixing two ionic solutions lets their cations and anions swap partners, and Solubility Rules gave you the tool to predict which pairings stay dissolved and which ones do not. A precipitation reaction is simply what happens when you put those two ideas together: it is a double replacement reaction where the solubility rules predict that at least one of the new pairings is insoluble. When that insoluble pairing forms, the ions that make it up come together into a solid lattice and drop out of solution, visible as cloudiness, a colored solid settling to the bottom, or a suspension you could filter out.

The classic example, sometimes nicknamed golden rain for the way bright yellow crystals drift down through a warm solution as it cools, is the reaction between lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide: Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2 KI(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2 KNO3(aq). Checking the balance atom by atom: 1 lead on each side, 2 nitrogens on each side (one Pb(NO3)2 unit contributes 2, and 2 KNO3 units contribute 2), 6 oxygens on each side, 2 potassiums on each side, and 2 iodines on each side (2 from KI on the left, 2 in PbI2 on the right). Applying the solubility rules from the previous chapter confirms the prediction: KNO3 combines a Group 1 cation with nitrate, both always soluble, so it remains dissolved, while PbI2 combines lead(II) with iodide, one of the documented halide exceptions, so it precipitates as a bright yellow solid.

Precipitation reactions are not just a classroom curiosity. Water treatment plants use them to remove dissolved metal contaminants by adding a reagent that forms an insoluble compound with the contaminant, which can then be filtered out. Chemists also use precipitation as a form of qualitative analysis, adding a known reagent to an unknown solution and using which precipitate forms, and its color, as a clue to which ions were originally present.

One detail worth flagging now: writing the reaction as Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2 KI(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2 KNO3(aq) is accurate, but it treats the dissolved reactants as if they existed as intact formula units in solution, when in reality they are fully separated into freely moving ions. The next two chapters rewrite this same reaction to show that more honestly.
